1289.title: The open tent
1289.hook: Abraham's tent, open on all sides, is the model of hospitality
1289.howItsDone: Hachnasat orchim is practiced by inviting guests, including strangers and travelers, to Shabbat and holiday meals, and some synagogues match visitors with host families.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bal tashchit, and its line, waste nothing. Today, a door that stays open.

Midday, in the plains of Mamre. Genesis says Abraham "sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." Not inside, in the shade. At the door. Then he looks up and sees three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait for them to knock or ask: "he ran to meet them from the tent door," and bowed to the ground. Abraham, in the worst heat of the day, running toward people he's never met. You met this scene in year one; today, the tent the rabbis saw behind it.
screen: `THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `SITTING AT THE DOOR.` → `HE RAN TO MEET THEM.`

segments.voice: Hachnasat orchim. Bringing in guests. First, the tent. The rabbis noticed that Abraham saw his guests before they reached him, and a collection called Avot de-Rabbi Natan says his tent had openings on every side, so a traveler from any direction would find a way in. No front door, no back door. Second, say little, do much. Abraham offers "a morsel of bread." Then he hurries to Sarah for cakes, runs to the herd for a calf, and sets out butter and milk. The Talmud, in tractate Bava Metzia, reads this as a habit of the righteous: they promise little and give much. Third, a startling ranking. Abraham says, "pass not away," and the rabbis read those words as spoken to God: please wait. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, draws a bold lesson from it: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the presence of God. Abraham left a vision to go set out bread. Fourth, the house today. In the Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers, the sage Yose ben Yochanan says to let your house be open wide, and to let the poor be members of your household. Not guests on a schedule; part of the family. The tent at Mamre becomes a way to keep any kitchen: see people early, go toward them, say less than you give. The door was the place Abraham chose to sit.
screen: `OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.` · `A MORSEL, THEN A FEAST.` · `GREATER THAN A VISION.` · `LET YOUR HOUSE BE OPEN WIDE.` · then, large: `OPEN TENT.`

segments.voice: Let the people around your life pass through your mind: a new neighbor, a colleague eating alone, a friend who's been quiet, a student far from home, and let one face stay. Ask what an open tent would look like for that person this week: a coffee, a seat at your table, a walk, an invitation before they have to ask. Settle on the morsel you'll offer, and quietly plan to give more than you said.
The open tent. Hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests: Abraham at the door, open on every side, running to meet strangers. Today's word.
Your line: open tent. No front door, no back door, a way in from every side. See you tomorrow.

1290.title: Block close: character is daily
1290.hook: the traits are built one day at a time
1290.howItsDone: In a Mussar group, a student may choose one trait to work on for a set stretch of time, practice a small daily act tied to it, and keep a short nightly journal of how the day went.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was open tent: see people early, go toward them, give more than you promise. Today, the last day of this block on Mussar and Jewish ethics.

A jar of sourdough starter sits on a kitchen counter. Flour and water, a little bubbly, a little sour. Its keeper feeds it every day. Skip a day, and it sulks. Skip a week, and it may not come back. No feeding is big enough to last a month. The starter lives on small, steady care, and in return it raises every loaf. Mussar treats character much the same way.
screen: `A JAR ON THE COUNTER.` → `FED EVERY DAY.` → `HOW CHARACTER STAYS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: First, the map. This block walked through traits as measures, each with a right size: humility, patience, gratitude, order, calm, silence, truth, trust, zeal, generosity, honor, responsibility. Then speech: harmful speech, tales, slander, and speaking good. Then the hard ones, anger and envy, and Luzzatto's ladder up to holiness. Then ethics in the world: honest weights, not stealing minds, fair work, animals, waste, and the open tent. Second, repetition. Maimonides, in his laws of character, says that a person who wants to change a trait should practice the opposite act, again and again, until it comes easily and becomes part of who they are. Not a vow. A habit. Third, a thousand coins. The Mishnah, in Ethics of the Fathers, says the world is judged by the abundance of deeds. Maimonides, commenting on it, gives an example: someone who gives a thousand coins to one person at one time doesn't build generosity the way someone does who gives one coin a thousand times. The trait grows from the number of acts, not the size of one. Fourth, no finish line. Rabbi Tarfon says, in the same tractate, that it isn't yours to complete the work, and you aren't free to stop doing it. That's why Mussar, as this block met it, meant one trait at a time, an accounting of the soul at night, and beginning again the next morning. None of these traits is learned in a day. Every one of them is learned daily.
screen: `TRAITS, SPEECH, LADDER, WORLD.` · `PRACTICE THE OPPOSITE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `ONE COIN A THOUSAND TIMES.` · `NOT YOURS TO COMPLETE, NOT FREE TO STOP.` · then, large: `CHARACTER IS DAILY.`

segments.voice: Let the traits from this block pass by: humility, patience, gratitude, truth, generosity, calm, speaking good, honest dealing, an open door. Notice which one tugs, not the most impressive but the one your days actually need, and choose it for the month ahead, shrunk to one small daily act: one thank-you, one honest sentence, one coin, one pause before answering. If you pray, ask for help with it in your own words.
Block close. Mussar and Jewish ethics: traits, speech, the ladder, and the world, built one act at a time. Today's word.
Your line: character is daily. Next comes a new block: the life cycle, from birth to death. A block done, one day at a time.

1291.title: Every season of a Jewish life
1291.hook: Jewish tradition marks every stage from birth to death
1291.carry: each season of life is marked and blessed
1291.howItsDone: Jewish life-cycle rituals are usually led by family and community together: a baby's naming in the synagogue or at home, a bar or bat mitzvah's first reading from the Torah, a wedding under the chuppah, and shiva, when mourners receive visitors at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was character is daily: one small act, repeated. Today a new block begins: the life cycle.

Pencil lines climb a kitchen doorframe. Each one has a name and a date beside it, scratched in on a birthday or the first day of school. Some families do this without being told to. They want to mark the moments when a life moves up a notch, so they don't slip by unnoticed. Judaism has its own doorframe, and it runs from a life's first days to its last, and beyond. Before stopping at any one mark, a look at the whole frame.
screen: `PENCIL LINES ON A DOORFRAME.` → `MARKING THE MOMENTS.` → `THE WHOLE FRAME.`

segments.voice: First, the seasons. Ecclesiastes says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." And then: "A time to be born, and a time to die." The tradition takes the seasons of a life seriously enough to give each one a ritual. Second, the marks. A new baby is welcomed with blessings and a name; for boys, with a covenant ceremony, the brit milah. A young person comes of age as a bar or bat mitzvah, a son or daughter of the commandments. Two people marry under a canopy, the chuppah. And at the end there are rituals for dying, for burial, and for the mourners who stay behind: days of sitting at home, called shiva, and the words of the kaddish. Third, a map in the Mishnah. In Ethics of the Fathers, Judah ben Tema lays out a life by ages: at five, scripture; at ten, Mishnah; at thirteen, the commandments; at eighteen, the wedding canopy; and on, through strength, understanding and counsel, to old age. It isn't a schedule anyone must keep. It's a picture of a life with stages, each with its own work. Fourth, one blessing for many doorways. Jewish tradition has a short blessing called shehecheyanu, said at new and joyful moments: a first fruit of the season, a holiday's first night, a new home, a new garment. It thanks God for keeping us alive and bringing us to this time. The rituals don't make the moments happen. They make sure a person stops, and notices, that they have.
screen: `A SEASON FOR EVERY THING.` · `BIRTH, COMING OF AGE, CANOPY, MOURNING.` · `A LIFE BY AGES.` · `A BLESSING FOR NEW MOMENTS.` · then, large: `A LIFE HAS RITUALS.`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning of your own life, as far back as you know: a naming, a blessing, a party, a photo, then a birthday that mattered, a graduation, a first job, a move, a wedding, a funeral you stood at. Let each mark come up like a pencil line on the doorframe, and notice which ones had a ritual and which passed with nothing to mark them. Notice, too, the next doorway ahead of you.
A life has rituals: birth, coming of age, marriage, mourning, each stage marked, and one blessing for the new moments in between. Today's word.

1292.title: Blessed Is the One Who Comes
1292.hook: blessings and visits greet a new baby
1292.carry: a new life is greeted with a blessing
1292.howItsDone: When a Jewish baby is born, families often recite a blessing of thanks, and in many communities friends gather at the home, such as at a shalom zachar, an Ashkenazi custom on the first Friday night after a boy's birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was a life has rituals: every stage marked, from first days to last. Today, the very first stage.

Bethlehem, at the end of the book of Ruth. A baby boy has just been born to Ruth and Boaz. The scene the book chooses to show isn't the birth. It's the neighbors. The women of the town crowd around Naomi, the grandmother, the one who came home bitter and empty-handed. They bless God for her. They tell her this child will restore her life and care for her when she's old. Naomi takes the baby and holds him to her chest. Then the women do one more thing: they give him his name, Obed. A child arrives, and the street shows up.
screen: `A BABY IN BETHLEHEM.` → `THE NEIGHBORS CROWD IN.` → `THEY BLESS, AND THEY NAME HIM.`

segments.voice: First, a blessing for good news. The Talmud teaches that on hearing good news that brings good to others as well as to you, you bless God as the one who is good and does good. Some authorities apply it to the birth of a child, a joy the whole household shares. Before the baby has done anything, the first response is gratitude. Second, the visit. In Ashkenazi custom, on the first Friday night after a boy is born, friends come to the family's home for a gathering called shalom zachar, welcome to the male: snacks, songs, words of Torah. Sephardi and other communities have their own customs, and families welcome girls with gatherings too, which you'll meet later this week. Nobody greets a new life alone. Third, the words at the door. When a baby is carried in to a ceremony, people often call out baruch haba, blessed is the one who comes. It echoes a line from the Psalms: "Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD." Fourth, back to Bethlehem. The women in Ruth don't just congratulate. They speak about the baby's future and about Naomi's healing. Welcome, in that story, is a promise: we see this child, and we see the family around him.

Then add one good thing you hope for them, a hope rather than advice, and if you pray, hold them in your prayer.

1293.title: The covenant of circumcision
1293.hook: a baby boy's circumcision on the eighth day
1293.howItsDone: Many Jewish families hold a brit milah on the eighth day after a boy's birth, with a mohel performing the circumcision, a sandak holding the baby, blessings, the announcement of his Hebrew name, and a festive meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was welcome: a blessing, friends at the house, and baruch haba at the door. Today, the ceremony that greeting so often opens.

A room full of people, on the eighth day after a birth: grandparents, cousins, a few friends who took the morning off. Near the front stands an empty chair that nobody sits in. The baby is carried in on a pillow, and the room calls out: baruch haba. One person, a grandfather perhaps, or an honored friend, settles in to hold the child on his lap. Another, trained for exactly this, steps forward. Then come blessings, a name spoken aloud for the first time, a little wine, and food.
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY.` → `AN EMPTY CHAIR.` → `A NAME SPOKEN ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Brit milah. Brit means covenant; milah means circumcision. First, the command and its day. In Genesis, in the chapter this path met in Lech Lecha, God makes a covenant with Abraham, to be carried in the body: "And he that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you." The eighth day is so central that the Talmud teaches it goes ahead even on Shabbat. But a baby's health comes first: if the child is unwell, the brit waits. Second, the people. The one who performs it is called a mohel. The one who holds the baby is the sandak, a place of honor. And the empty chair belongs to Elijah the prophet. Tradition says Elijah once complained that Israel had abandoned the covenant, so he is invited to every brit, to see for himself that it goes on. Third, the words. The father, or both parents, bless God for the command to bring the child into the covenant of Abraham. The guests answer with a line from the liturgy: as he has entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, the wedding canopy, and good deeds. Learning, love, kindness: a whole life, wished for in one breath. Fourth, the name. At the brit, the boy's Hebrew name is announced for the first time, as son of his father, and in some families his mother too. The covenant is the frame; the name is what goes inside it.

Then let the last image rest: a whole room promising to stand behind one small person. If you pray, you can pray for a child you love.

1294.title: A Name Handed Down
1294.hook: Ashkenazim often name after relatives who have died, Sephardim often after living grandparents
1294.carry: a child's name carries a loved one forward
1294.howItsDone: Ashkenazi Jews often name a baby after a relative who has died, while Sephardi Jews often name children after living grandparents; the Hebrew name is announced at a brit milah or a naming for a girl.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was brit milah, and your line was the covenant. At the end of that morning, a name was spoken aloud for the first time. Where does a name like that come from?

Two families, two baby boys, the same week. In the first, the baby is named after his great-grandfather, who died last spring. When the name is announced, his grandmother starts to cry, and then to laugh. In the second, the baby is named after his grandfather, who is standing right there in the front row, holding the camera and suddenly unable to work it. Two customs, two very different moments, and underneath both, the same conviction.
screen: `A NAME FROM THE ONE WHO DIED.` → `A NAME FROM THE ONE IN THE FRONT ROW.` → `THE SAME CONVICTION.`

segments.voice: First, the Ashkenazi custom. Jews whose families come from Central and Eastern Europe have often named children after relatives who have died, and often avoided naming after anyone still living. The name becomes a way to keep someone present: a grandmother who never met the baby is named aloud every time the child is called to dinner. Second, the Sephardi custom. Jews whose families come from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East have often done the opposite: they name children after living grandparents. To hear your own name given to a grandchild, while you're alive to hear it, is a great honor. One custom carries the dead forward. The other crowns the living. Both say a child doesn't arrive from nowhere. Third, the old roots. In Genesis, when Jacob blesses his grandsons, he asks that his own name, and the names of Abraham and Isaac, be named in them. Long before either custom, a grandfather wanted to live on in the children's names. And Proverbs puts it plainly: "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches." Fourth, the name you earn. A midrash teaches that every person has three names: the one their parents give, the one other people call them, and the one they acquire for themselves, and the last is the best. The family can hand down a name. Only a life can fill it.

1295.title: Welcoming a daughter
1295.howItsDone: Jewish families welcome a baby girl in different ways: a naming when her father is called to the Torah in Ashkenazi synagogues, a zeved habat with verses from the Song of Songs in Sephardi communities, or a home ceremony called simchat bat.

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was names carry people: named for the ones who died, or for the ones still here. Today, the end of the week, and a daughter's name.

"Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice." A line from the Song of Songs. In the poem, a lover calls to someone hidden, a dove in the clefts of the rock: come out, let me see you. In some Sephardi homes, those words are sung over a baby girl, days or weeks old, while the family gathers around her. The dove in the rock is a daughter who has just arrived, and the whole room is saying: we want to see you, we want to hear you.

segments.voice: Simchat bat. The joy of a daughter. First, the naming at the Torah. In traditional Ashkenazi synagogues, a girl's name is given when her father is called up to the Torah reading. A blessing is said for the mother's health and for the baby, and her Hebrew name is spoken for the first time, there, in front of the open scroll. Second, the Sephardi gift. Sephardi communities hold a ceremony called zeved habat, the gift of the daughter. Verses from the Song of Songs are sung, the dove in the rock among them, and a blessing asks that she grow in health and goodness. A daughter is received the way you receive a gift. Third, the newer ceremonies. Families across different kinds of communities now hold a home ceremony called simchat bat. There's no single script: families choose readings, light candles, wrap the baby in a prayer shawl, tell the story of her name. Some recall Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah. The details vary from home to home. The aim doesn't: a girl should be greeted with as much joy as a boy. Fourth, the week, looked back on. An open tent. Character built daily. A life with rituals. A welcome at the door. A covenant on the eighth day. Names that carry people. And now, a daughter, seen and heard. Side by side, the week says one thing: a new person is met at the door, by name, out loud.
